nameStory: The name 'cranesbill' comes from the plant's distinctive fruit, which has a long, straight projection that looks remarkably like a crane's bill! This beak-like structure is actually the plant's style - the part that connects to the flower's reproductive organs. The 'northern' part of the name reflects this species' preference for cooler northern forests and woodlands.
description: Northern cranesbill is a small annual or biennial wildflower that grows close to the ground in forest clearings and burned areas. This hairy little plant reaches about knee-high with sprawling stems that may stand upright or trail along the ground. Its deeply divided leaves look almost hand-like, and it produces tiny lavender flowers followed by the distinctive crane's-bill-shaped fruits that give it its name.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: The unmistakable crane's-bill-shaped fruit has a rounded base with a straight, pointed 'beak' about an inch long - it really does look like a bird's bill when you see it!

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny lavender or pale pink flowers appear singly or in pairs, each with five notched petals that look like they've been snipped with scissors at the tips

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Palmate leaves are deeply divided into 5-7 finger-like lobes, each further divided into smaller teeth - they feel slightly rough and hairy to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Sprawling annual with hairy, reddish stems that may grow upright or trail along the ground, rarely getting taller than 18 inches

habitat: Look for northern cranesbill in recently disturbed forest areas, especially sites that have burned within the last few years. It thrives in forest clearings, along woodland edges, and in areas where the tree canopy has been opened up by natural disturbances. This sun-loving plant prefers well-drained soils in mixed and coniferous forests throughout New England's mountainous regions.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring as soil warms, with young plants developing their characteristic deeply-lobed leaves.
seasonality.summer: Small lavender flowers bloom from June through August, quickly followed by the distinctive crane's-bill fruits that make identification easy.
seasonality.fall: Mature fruits split open explosively to scatter seeds, while the annual plants begin to die back as temperatures cool.
seasonality.winter: Seeds lie dormant in the soil, sometimes for decades or even centuries, waiting for the next fire or disturbance to trigger germination.

funFact: Northern cranesbill seeds can lie buried and dormant in forest soil for centuries - some may have been waiting since before European settlement! They only wake up when a forest fire burns away the leaf litter above them, allowing sunlight to trigger their dramatic germination.
confusionNotes: The deeply-lobed leaves can look surprisingly similar to some members of the buttercup family, including toxic monkshood and larkspur species. However, northern cranesbill's distinctive crane's-bill fruits are a dead giveaway - no buttercup family plant has anything like them!
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse wild cranesbills with the colorful potted 'geraniums' sold at garden centers - those are actually pelargoniums from South Africa! True geraniums like northern cranesbill are much more subtle plants with smaller flowers and that distinctive beaked fruit.
compareHints: Northern cranesbill is much smaller and more delicate than wild geranium, with tiny lavender flowers instead of large pink ones. Unlike the weedy Herb Robert with its strong musky smell and deeply cut ferny leaves, northern cranesbill has less divided leaves and no distinctive odor. The key difference from all its relatives is its preference for recently burned or disturbed forest sites.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wild geranium stands out from its cranesbill cousins by its substantial size, soft pink flowers, and preference for rich woodlands.
Among New England's wild geraniums, Herb Robert is the most delicate and lacy-looking, with much more finely divided leaves than the larger Wild Geranium.
Among New England's crane's-bills, bloody crane's-bill stands out for its deeply divided leaves that are cut almost to the base, creating very narrow segments.
Among New England's crane's-bills, rock crane's-bill is unique for its low, mat-forming growth and intensely fragrant leaves - most others grow more upright and have much less scented foliage.
Thunberg's Geranium is much smaller and more delicate than our common Wild Geranium, with more finely divided leaves and smaller flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Carolina crane's-bill has the smallest flowers - much tinier than the showy inch-wide blooms of wild geranium or the medium-sized flowers of Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, meadow crane's-bill is one of the largest and most robust, forming much bigger clumps than most relatives.

Among New England's crane's-bills, dusky crane's-bill is unique for its nearly black flowers with backward-curved petals - our native wild geranium has pink flowers that face upward, while Herb Robert has small bright pink flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, dove's-foot stands out for its exceptionally soft, velvety leaf texture and low, mat-forming growth habit.
Among New England's crane's-bills, this is one of the tiniest and most easily overlooked.
Purple-vein geranium stands out from other New England geraniums primarily by its bright blue flowers - most other species have pink, white, or purple blooms.

Among New England's crane's-bills, cut-leaved crane's-bill stands out for having the most finely divided leaves - while wild geranium has broader, less deeply cut leaves and Herb Robert has more triangular leaf segments, cut-leaved crane's-bill looks almost feathery.
Among New England's crane's-bills, little-robin is the tiniest - much smaller than wild geranium or Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Long-stalked stands out for its exceptionally long flower stalks and deeply dissected leaves.

Richardson's geranium differs from New England's common wild geranium by having paler flowers with more prominent dark veining, perfectly straight (not curved) seed beaks, and more finely divided leaf segments.
Wood crane's-bill differs from our native wild geranium by having more deeply dissected leaves and typically stronger purple coloring with more prominent petal veining.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Siberian Crane's-bill would be one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
